modules.title: Rook endings: the key positions at depth
modules.summary: Lucena, Philidor, the short side and Vancura as exact knowledge: the method for each side and the move that decides.
modules.source: Dvoretsky, Dvoretsky's Endgame Manual, ch. 9 (Lucena, Philidor, flank checks, Vancura); de la Villa, 100 Endgames You Must Know, ch. 9; every position checked with Stockfish 16 at depth 22-28

lessons.title: Lucena: build the bridge
lessons.objective: Win the Lucena position: cut the king off, put the rook on the fourth rank, and block the last check with the rook.

sections.md:
The Lucena position is the target of most winning rook-and-pawn endings. White has a pawn on the seventh rank, the king on the queening square, and the black king cut off from the pawn by at least one file. Black's rook waits to check.

The win has three steps.

1. Check the defending king one more file away (1.Rd1+ Ke7). Now it cannot return to the c-file.
2. Put the rook on the fourth rank (2.Rd4). This is the bridge.
3. Bring the king out on the side of the defending king. Black checks from behind. The king steps down the board, and when it reaches the fifth rank, the rook blocks the next check on b4.

The fourth rank is the right rank because the king stops on the fifth. The rook interposes one rank below the king, and the checks end.

Do not rush the pawn. Until the king is out, the pawn needs the king for protection.

sections.caption: The Lucena position. 1.Rd1+ Ke7 2.Rd4: the rook takes the fourth rank and waits. Then the king walks out (Kc7, Kb6, Kc6, Kb5) and Rb4 blocks the last check.

sections.prompt: The same position on the other wing. Promote the g-pawn within 14 moves against the engine.
sections.tip: 1.Re1+ first, then Re4. The king comes out via f7, then g6 or f6 and g5; the rook blocks the last check on g4.

sections.question: White to move. Black has just checked on b1. Which move wins?
options: 7.Rb4: block the check with the rook
7.Ka4: walk away from the checks
7.Kc4: run towards the centre
7.Ka5: step to the edge
sections.explanation: 7.Rb4 ends the checks and the pawn promotes. After 7.Ka4, 7.Kc4 or 7.Ka5 Black plays ...Rxb7 and it is a draw (Stockfish 16: 0.00 for all three). This is why the rook went to the fourth rank.

lessons.title: Philidor: the third-rank defence
lessons.objective: Hold rook and pawn against rook with the rook on your third rank, and switch to checks from behind when the pawn advances.

sections.md:
When the defending king stands in front of the pawn, the Philidor defence draws. It has two parts.

1. While the pawn is on its fifth rank, keep the rook on your own third rank (for Black, the sixth rank). If the white king steps up to that rank, the rook checks it, and the king has no shelter.
2. When White pushes the pawn to the sixth rank, the king loses its shelter in front of the pawn. Now drop the rook to the first rank and check from behind. The king cannot escape the checks and still protect the pawn.

The defence needs no calculation. Wait on the third rank, then check from behind. Your king stays on the queening square or next to it.

In the position below, Stockfish 16 gives 0.00 for each of White's eight best moves. The drill asks you to prove it at the board.

sections.caption: The Philidor position, White to move. The rook on a6 guards the sixth rank: Kd6 or Ke6 runs into a check. After e5-e6 the rook goes to a1 and checks from behind.

sections.prompt: Hold the draw as Black. Make a draw by repetition, or win the pawn.
sections.tip: Rook to the sixth rank (Rb6). When f5-f6 comes, rook to the first rank and check from behind. Keep the king on f8, g8 or f7.

sections.question: In the Philidor defence, when must the defending rook leave its third rank?
options: When the pawn advances to the sixth rank
When the attacking king reaches its fifth rank
Never: the rook stays on the third rank until the pawn falls
When the attacking rook reaches the seventh rank
sections.explanation: While the pawn is on the fifth rank, the rook keeps the white king off the sixth. When the pawn reaches the sixth, the king can no longer hide in front of it, so checks from behind work: the rook drops to the first rank at once.

lessons.title: The short side and the long side
lessons.objective: When the king must leave the pawn's file, send it to the short side and keep the rook on the long side for flank checks.

sections.md:
The pawn divides the board into two parts. The short side has fewer files between the pawn and the edge. The long side has more. With a c-pawn, the short side is the a- and b-files; the long side runs from d to h.

When the defending king is pushed away from the pawn, send it to the short side. The rook then works on the long side, far from the pawn. From there it checks the attacking king from the flank. The king cannot come close to the rook without leaving its pawn.

If the defending king goes to the long side instead, it stands between its own rook and the pawn. The attacking king then walks to the short side, where the black rook has no room to check, and shelters the pawn.

Rule of thumb from the endgame manuals: flank checks need the rook at least three files away from the pawn. A rook on the g-file against a c-pawn is four files away.

sections.caption: Black to move after Rh7+. The c-pawn leaves two files on the short side (a, b) and five on the long side (d to h). The black rook on g1 already stands on the long side.

sections.question: Black to move. Two of these king moves hold the draw. Which one loses?
sections.explanation: 1...Kd8? goes to the long side. 2.Kc6! and the white king shelters the pawn: 2...Rc1 3.Rh8+ Ke7 4.Rc8 Rc2 5.Kb7, then c5-c6. Stockfish 16 at depth 28: about +5 for White. After 1...Kb8 (short side) or 1...Kc8 (in front of the pawn) the rook keeps its checks from the long side: 0.00.

sections.prompt: Hold the draw as Black from the same position. Make a draw by repetition, or win the pawn.
sections.tip: King to b8 or c8. Keep the rook far away on the long side and check the white king from the flank whenever it comes up beside the pawn.

sections.question: White has a pawn on the f-file. The black king is driven off f8. Where do the black king and rook belong?
options: King to g7 or h7; rook on the a-file
King to e7; rook on the h-file
King to e7; rook on the a-file
King to g7; rook on the h-file
sections.explanation: For an f-pawn the short side is the g- and h-files and the long side runs from a to e. King to the short side, rook to the far end of the long side: the a-rook is five files from the pawn and checks the king from the flank.

lessons.title: Vancura: the rook pawn on the sixth
lessons.objective: Draw against a rook pawn on the sixth with the white rook in front of it: attack the pawn from the side and keep the king on g7 or h7.

sections.md:
Rook ending, a-pawn on the sixth, the white rook in front of it on a8. The white rook blocks its own pawn. Vancura's defence uses that.

1. The black rook attacks the pawn from the side, along the sixth rank (Rf6). The white rook is tied to the a-file.
2. The black king waits on g7 or h7. From there it guards g8 and h8, so when the pawn reaches a7 the white rook has no check on the eighth rank and no Rh8.
3. If the white king walks towards the pawn, the rook checks it and returns to the sixth rank.
4. If the pawn goes to a7, the rook goes behind it (Ra6 or lower on the a-file).

The king square is the detail that decides. On g7 or h7 the king is safe. On f7 the rook move Rh8 wins: if ...Rxa7, then Rh7+ skewers king and rook. On g6, a6-a7 threatens Rg8+ and a8=Q.

sections.caption: Vancura's position, Black to move. The rook on f6 attacks a6 from the side; the king on g7 guards g8 and h8.

sections.question: Black to move. Two of these moves hold the draw. Which one loses?
sections.explanation: 1...Kg6? 2.a7! and White threatens Rg8+ followed by a8=Q. Stockfish 16 finds a forced mate for White after 2.a7. With the king on g7 or h7 the rook cannot check on the eighth rank, and 1...Kh7 or 1...Rf4+ keeps the balance (0.0).

sections.prompt: Hold the draw as Black. Make a draw by repetition, or win the pawn.
sections.tip: Rook on the sixth rank attacking a6, king on g7 or h7. When the white king comes near the pawn, check it from the side and return to the sixth rank.

sections.prompt: White to move. The black king stands on f7, one square too far from g7. Win.
sections.hint: With the king on f7, h8 is free for the rook, and the seventh rank is open for a skewer.
sections.explanation: 1.Rh8! threatens a8=Q. 1...Rxa7 2.Rh7+ skewers the king and the rook on the seventh rank. Stockfish 16: about +5 after 1.Rh8, 0.00 after any king move. With the black king on g7 the same move fails, because g7 attacks h8.

modules.title: Bishop, queen and rook: exact positions
modules.summary: The wrong bishop and the corner, the queen against a pawn on the seventh, and the queen against the rook: positions where one move decides.
modules.source: Dvoretsky, Dvoretsky's Endgame Manual, ch. 4 (bishop against pawns), 8 and 12-13 (queen against pawns and against rook); de la Villa, 100 Endgames You Must Know, ch. 1 and 3; every position checked with the Syzygy tablebases (4 pieces) and Stockfish 16

lessons.title: The wrong bishop and the corner
lessons.objective: With a rook pawn and the wrong bishop, keep the defending king out of the corner, or, as the defender, find the one route into it.

sections.md:
A rook pawn and a bishop that does not control the queening square: the wrong bishop. If the defending king reaches the corner in front of the pawn, the game is a draw. The king cannot be driven out, and the pawn cannot pass it.

So the whole fight is about the corner.

1. The attacker uses the bishop to take away the squares on the way to the corner. With an h-pawn and a light-squared bishop, the bishop can take g8 (and f7, h7). The pawn, once on h6, takes g7.
2. The defender counts the route: which squares lead to h8, g8 or g7, and which of them the bishop or the pawn can cover in time.

In these positions there is usually one right move. The tablebase confirms both challenges below: every other move changes the result.

sections.caption: The fortress. The bishop can never control h8, a dark square. The black king goes back and forth between h8 and g8; if the bishop takes g8 away while the king is on h8, it is stalemate.

sections.prompt: White to move. Only one move wins: the tablebase says every other move draws.
sections.hint: The black king wants g8 or g7. Which of those can the bishop take away right now?
sections.explanation: 1.Bc4! takes f7 and g8. After 1...Kf8 2.h6 the king cannot use g7 (the pawn) or g8 (the bishop). After 1...Ke7 2.h6 Kf6 3.Bd3 Kf7 4.Bh7 the bishop shuts the king out. Any other first move lets the king reach the corner in time.

sections.prompt: Black to move. Only one move draws: find the route to the corner.
sections.hint: f8 looks closest to h8, but which squares next to it can White cover?
sections.explanation: 1...Kf6! heads for g7, a dark square the bishop can never control. 1...Kf8? 2.h6 and the king is shut out: g8 belongs to the bishop on c4, g7 to the pawn. 1...Kf6 2.h6 Kg6 or 2.Bg8 Kg7: the king reaches the corner.

sections.question: White has a bishop and an a-pawn. Which bishop wins if the black king stands in the corner in front of the pawn?
options: A light-squared bishop, because a8 is a light square
A dark-squared bishop, because a1 is a dark square
Neither: the king in the corner always draws
Either bishop: the pawn is enough
sections.explanation: The queening square of an a-pawn for White is a8, a light square. A light-squared bishop can drive the king out of a8; a dark-squared bishop never can, and the king in the corner draws.

lessons.title: Queen against a pawn on the seventh
lessons.objective: Know when the queen beats a pawn on the seventh rank, and bring the king into the winning zone against a bishop pawn.

sections.md:
Queen against a pawn on the seventh rank, the defending king next to its pawn.

Against a centre pawn or a knight pawn, the queen wins however far away the white king is, as long as the queen can stop the pawn at once. The method: check and pin until the defending king must stand in front of its pawn. The pawn is blocked for one move. Use that tempo to bring your king one step closer. Repeat.

Against a bishop pawn or a rook pawn the method fails, because of stalemate. With a c-pawn the defending king goes to the corner (...Ka1): if the queen takes the pawn, it is stalemate. With an a-pawn, the king in front of the pawn has no moves at all.

So against the bishop pawn and the rook pawn the queen wins only when its own king is already close: inside the winning zone. There, the king arrives in time to set up a mate or to take the pawn without stalemate. Often only one king move gets there in time.

sections.caption: The stalemate trick. Black has played ...Ka1 and left the c-pawn to the queen. 1.Qxc2 is stalemate: a2, b1 and b2 are all covered.

sections.question: Black has a pawn on the seventh rank, the black king beside it, and the white king is far away. Against which pawn does the queen still win?
options: A d-pawn
A c-pawn
An a-pawn
An f-pawn
sections.explanation: Centre and knight pawns lose to the queen whatever the distance: the defending king must step in front of the pawn, and White gains a tempo each time. Against bishop pawns (c, f) and rook pawns (a, h) the defender has stalemate, and only a close white king wins.

sections.prompt: White to move. The tablebase says only one move wins. Find it.
sections.hint: The queen cannot win alone. Which king move is one tempo faster towards c3 and d3?
sections.explanation: 1.Kd5! The king heads for c4 and d3, and the queen gains time with checks and pins until it arrives (for example 1...Kd2 2.Qb2 Kd3 3.Qd4+ Ke2 4.Qc3 and the pawn falls). 1.Ke5 or 1.Kd6 is one tempo too slow, and the stalemate defence holds.

lessons.title: Queen against rook
lessons.objective: Win with queen against rook: drive the king to the edge and catch the rook the moment it leaves its king.

sections.md:
Queen against rook is a win, but it is slow work. The defender keeps the rook next to the king, where the king protects it, and gives checks whenever he can.

The method:

1. Drive the defending king to the edge with king and queen together. The queen alone cannot do it.
2. Bring your king close. The rook then has fewer safe squares.
3. Use zugzwang. When the rook must move away from its king, look for the fork: a queen check that also attacks the rook.

Two patterns finish the game: the fork (check plus attack on the loose rook) and the skewer (a check on the line between king and rook). The defender's hopes are stalemate and a rook sacrifice that forces it, so check every move for stalemate.

sections.caption: The rook on a5 is far from its king. 1.Qb6+ checks along the sixth rank and attacks the rook on the diagonal: the fork.

sections.question: In queen against rook, where is the rook safest?
options: Next to its own king
Far away, on the opposite edge
On the same line as both kings
On the long diagonal
sections.explanation: Next to its king the rook is protected, and no fork wins it. Far from the king it is loose: a queen check that also attacks it wins it at once.

sections.prompt: Win the rook (or mate) within 20 moves. The rook stands next to its king; make it leave.
sections.tip: Qe8+ pushes the king into the corner. Then improve the queen with tempo; sooner or later the rook must leave b7. When it does, look for a check that also hits it.

sections.prompt: White to move. The rook on a4 has strayed from its king. Win it.
sections.hint: Find a check on a line through the king that also touches a4.
sections.explanation: 1.Qd7+ checks on the d-file and attacks a4 on the diagonal d7-a4. 1...Rd4 2.Qxd4+ or any king move and 2.Qxa4. Stockfish 16 finds mate in 8 after 1.Qd7+; the next best move is worth less than three pawns.

modules.title: Calculation: candidates, comparison, the end of the line
modules.summary: Aagaard's method on master games: list every candidate first, calculate forcing lines to a position you can judge, and compare lines that look alike.
modules.source: Aagaard, Grandmaster Preparation: Calculation (ch. 1 candidate moves, ch. 4 comparison); Kotov, Think Like a Grandmaster (the tree of analysis); Rotlewi-Rubinstein, Lodz 1907; Averbakh-Kotov, Zurich 1953; Kasparov-Karpov, World Championship 1986 game 16; engine checks with Stockfish 16 at depth 22

lessons.title: Candidate moves: include the impossible move
lessons.objective: List every forcing candidate, including the move that leaves your queen en prise, before you calculate any of them.

sections.md:
Aagaard's first rule of calculation: find the candidates before you calculate. Most calculation errors are not miscalculations. They are the move you never looked at.

A working routine:

1. List every check, capture and threat for you, then for the opponent.
2. Add the moves your instinct rejects: a queen left en prise, a rook offered for nothing, a quiet move in the middle of an attack.
3. Only now calculate, one line at a time, to a position you can evaluate.

Rubinstein's win against Rotlewi (Lodz 1907) is the model. White attacks the black queen; the natural reply moves it. Rubinstein's list contained the capture 22...Rxc3, which leaves the queen where it stands, and then 23...Rd2, which offers the second rook. Stockfish 16 at depth 22 rates both as the best moves on the board by a wide margin.

sections.prompt: Black to move. 22.g3 attacks the queen on h4. List your candidates first, then play the strongest move.
sections.hint: The queen does not have to move. Count the defenders of e4.
sections.explanation: 22...Rxc3!! removes the knight that guards e4. 23.gxh4 Rd2!! and the queen can no longer hold e4. After the engine's 23.Bxb7 Rxg3 the attack goes on. Stockfish 16 at depth 22: about six pawns for Black after 22...Rxc3, about three after the safe 22...Qe7.

sections.prompt: Black to move, a queen down after 23.gxh4. Find the win.
sections.hint: The white queen on e2 guards e4. Give it a second job.
sections.explanation: 23...Rd2!! deflects the queen: 24.Qxd2 Bxe4+ 25.Qg2 Rh3 and mate on h2. 24.Rf2 Bxe4+ is no better. Stockfish 16 finds mate in 9. The natural 23...Bxe4+? 24.Qxe4 leaves White about three pawns better.

lessons.title: Calculate to a clear end: Kotov's queen sacrifice
lessons.objective: Calculate a forcing sacrifice until the opponent has no forcing replies left, and judge the position you reach.

sections.md:
Kotov described the tree of analysis: name the candidates, calculate each branch once, and stop at a position you can evaluate. Aagaard adds the stop rule: a forcing line is finished only when the opponent has no checks, captures or threats left.

Averbakh-Kotov (Zurich 1953) is the test. The centre is closed and the white king on h2 looks safe. But Black's queen on d7 eyes h3, the pawn on f4 takes g3 from the white king, and the rook on f6 can swing to h6.

30...Qxh3+ 31.Kxh3 Rh6+ 32.Kg4 Nf6+ 33.Kf5 drags the king to the fifth rank. The line does not end in mate. It ends in a position where the king cannot go back, Black's pieces surround it, and White has no counter-threat. That is enough to evaluate.

At depth 22, Stockfish 16 rates 30...Qxh3+ at about +2.5 for Black, against +1.1 for the quiet 30...b5. At lower depth it rates the sacrifice as a draw: the win is deep, and Kotov found it at the board.

sections.hint: The white king on f5 has few squares. Which rook check uses the open f-file?
sections.explanation: 34...Rf8+! 35.Kg4 Nf6+ 36.Kf5 and the knight checks again: the king cannot escape the net. Stockfish 16 at depth 22: about +4 for Black after 34...Rf8+, 0.00 after 34...Bxg5. Kotov repeated the knight checks and won with 43...Bxg5.

sections.question: When is a forcing line finished, in Aagaard's sense?
options: When the opponent has no checks, captures or threats left, and you can evaluate the position
When you have found a mate
After five moves for each side
When you have won back the material you gave
sections.explanation: Stop when the forcing moves run out and judge the position. Kotov's line after 30...Qxh3+ ends with the king on f5 and no white counterplay: that is a position you can evaluate, even without a mate in sight.

lessons.title: Comparison: four checks, one winner
lessons.objective: When several candidates look alike, calculate each to the point where they differ and compare the positions you reach.

sections.md:
Aagaard's comparison method: when two or more candidates look alike, calculate each to the point where they differ, then compare those positions. Do not stop at "both are checks".

Kasparov-Karpov, game 16 of the 1986 World Championship. Both sides attacked for twenty moves. Black's passed pawn on d3 is two steps from queening. White has several checks, and most of them lose: when the checks run out, the d-pawn promotes.

The routine:

1. Name every candidate. On move 37 White has four checks.
2. For each, find Black's best reply and the moment the line differs from the others.
3. Compare the end positions. Include Black's threat ...d2 in every evaluation.

sections.prompt: White to move. Black's queen has come back to e7, and the pawn on d3 is dangerous. Compare 35.d6 and 35.Rxg6, then play the better move.
sections.hint: Which move creates a threat Black must answer at once?
sections.explanation: 35.Rxg6! The f7-pawn is pinned by the queen on f4, so the rook cannot be taken, and 36.Rg8 is mate if Black ignores it. Stockfish 16 at depth 22: about +5.5 after 35.Rxg6, about -2.7 after 35.d6, when ...Qf6 and ...d2 come first.

sections.question: White to move. Four checks: 37.d6+, 37.Nf5+, 37.Qxe5+ and 37.Re8+. Which one wins?
sections.explanation: 37.d6+! Ke6 38.Re8+ Kd5 39.Rxe5+ Nxe5 40.d7 and the pawn decides. Stockfish 16 at depth 22: about +6 after 37.d6+, and about -4.5 or worse after each of the other three checks, because the d3-pawn promotes when the checks run out.

modules.title: Defence and counterattack in master games
modules.summary: When the opponent's pieces are committed to one wing, hit back in the centre or on the other wing, and calculate the counter-blow as precisely as an attack.
modules.source: Bronstein, Zurich International Chess Tournament 1953 (Geller-Euwe, Keres-Smyslov); Dvoretsky and Yusupov school, Boost Your Chess 3 (ch. 3 counterplay, ch. 7 counter-attack, ch. 14 defence); engine checks with Stockfish 16 at depth 22

lessons.title: Counterattack where the attacker is not
lessons.objective: Answer a kingside attack with a counter-blow on the second rank, and calculate it to the end.

sections.md:
A strong attack commits pieces to one wing. The defender's chance lies where those pieces are not.

Geller-Euwe (Zurich 1953). Geller lifted a rook to h4, took on h7 with the queen and played Bh6. White's queen, rook, bishop and knight are all on the kingside.

Euwe gave a rook (22...Rh8 23.Qxh8) to bring the other rook to c2. Now ...Rxg2+ and the queen's entry give Black full counterplay, while the white queen sits on h8, far from her king. Stockfish 16 rates the position equal; Geller's 24.Rc1? lost at once.

Three questions for the defender:

1. Where are the attacker's pieces? Where are they not?
2. Which of my pieces can reach the empty side in one move?
3. Is my counter-blow faster than his attack? Count the moves, as an attacker would.

lessons.title: Strike in the centre
lessons.objective: Meet a flank attack with a central counter-blow that creates threats faster than the attack.

sections.md:
Old rule, still true: a flank attack is best met by a counter-blow in the centre. The centre is where the attacker's pieces came from. When they leave, it opens.

Keres-Smyslov (Zurich 1953). Keres lifted both rooks to the h-file. 20.Rxh7 is coming, and Black's king has few defenders.

Smyslov did not defend h7. He took on c4 and pushed the c-pawn to c3. The pawn hits the bishop on b2, and soon the d4-pawn falls to the queen. Each move creates a threat, so White never has time to finish the attack.

To find such a counter-blow:

1. Look at the squares the attacker's pieces left behind.
2. Find the pawn break that opens them.
3. Calculate it as a race: count the moves to his mate and to your threats.

lessons.title: Defend with counter-threats: Lasker at 65
lessons.objective: In a passive position, put every piece on a square where it defends and threatens at once, and give material back when that turns defence into attack.

sections.md:
Lasker-style defence is not waiting. It is finding, for every piece, a square where it guards something and attacks something.

Euwe-Lasker (Zurich 1934). Lasker, 65, accepts a cramped position. His knight travels d5, b4, c2, his rooks go to the d-file and the second rank, his queen to g5. Each piece defends and attacks at the same time.

When Euwe attacks with h4-h5 and 35.Ne4, Lasker answers with counter-threats:

1. 35...Qxe5 takes a pawn and attacks the knight on e4. Its only defender, the rook on e1, is attacked by the knight on c2.
2. After 36.Nf6+ he gives the queen: 36...Qxf6 37.Rxf6 Nxf6. Material is level (two rooks and two knights against queen, rook and bishop), and every black piece is active.

Stockfish 16 at depth 22 rates both moves as clearly best: about +1.4 for Black, against about -0.9 and -4.7 for the alternatives.

modules.title: Model games: prophylaxis and the exchange sacrifice
modules.summary: Petrosian's exchange sacrifices and Karpov's prophylaxis: give material for squares, and stop the opponent's plan before you pursue your own.
modules.source: Dvoretsky and Yusupov school, Boost Your Chess 3 (ch. 12 prophylactic thinking); Nimzowitsch, My System (prophylaxis, blockade); games Reshevsky-Petrosian, Zurich 1953; Petrosian-Spassky, World Championship 1966 game 10; Karpov-Spassky, Candidates 1974 game 9; Karpov-Unzicker, Nice Olympiad 1974; engine checks with Stockfish 16

lessons.title: The exchange for a blockade: Petrosian
lessons.objective: Give the exchange to stop the opponent's centre pawns and win a permanent square for a knight.

sections.md:
A rook is worth more than a minor piece when lines are open. When the position is blocked, a well-placed knight can match a rook.

Petrosian used this more than anyone. Reshevsky-Petrosian (Zurich 1953): White has two bishops and the centre pawns d4 and e5. White's plan is d4-d5 and e5-e6, opening lines for the bishops.

Petrosian played 25...Re6, offering the rook for the light-squared bishop. After 26.a4 Ne7 27.Bxe6 fxe6, the pawn on e6 stops the e-pawn, the knight goes to d5, and no white piece can drive it away. White's rooks find no way in.

Stockfish 16 at depth 22 rates 25...Re6 as Black's best move. The game was drawn. That was the point: the sacrifice turned a worse position into a holdable one.

Ask before you give the exchange: which enemy pawns will stop, which square will be mine for good, and which of his rooks will have no file?

A direct attack on the white king
Two pawns and an extra tempo
A passed a-pawn

lessons.title: Two exchange sacrifices: Petrosian-Spassky 1966
lessons.objective: Give the exchange for light squares and a passive enemy, then finish when every black piece is tied down.

sections.md:
Game 10 of the 1966 World Championship. Petrosian, the champion, gives the exchange twice and wins with a queen sacrifice.

The first sacrifice, 21.Ne3, lets Black take the rook on f1 with the bishop. In return the knight comes to e3, where it controls f5, g4 and d5, and Black loses his light-squared bishop, the defender of those squares. Stockfish 16 at depth 22 agrees: about +0.3 for White after 21.Ne3, about -0.6 after the next best move.

The second, 24.Rxf4, removes the knight from f4. After 25.Be6+ the black rooks and queen are tied to f7 and the d6-pawn, and the white knights come to e4 and d6.

The final 30.Qh8+ is a short calculation. The positional work before it is the lesson: the light squares, the passive black rooks and the knights.

lessons.title: Prophylaxis: Karpov's quiet moves
lessons.objective: Before you make your plan, ask what the opponent wants, and choose the move that improves your worst piece while it takes his idea away.

sections.md:
Dvoretsky's prophylactic question: what does my opponent want to do, and what would he play if it were his move? Karpov asked it every move.

Two of his quiet moves from 1974:

1. Karpov-Spassky, Candidates game 9: 24.Nb1. The knight on c3 does nothing and blocks the c-pawn. From b1 it goes to d2 and f3, where it hits e5; the c-pawn is free to play c3 and push the black knight from b4. Stockfish 16 at depth 22 rates 24.Nb1 as the best move.
2. Karpov-Unzicker, Nice Olympiad: 24.Ba7. The a-file is the only open file. The bishop stands in front of Black's rook, so White doubles rooks behind it and Black can never contest the file. Stockfish 16 at depth 22 also rates it as the best move (about +0.8).

Neither move attacks anything. Each improves a piece and takes away the opponent's only active plan.

sections.question: Karpov's 24.Nb1 retreats a knight to the back rank. What is the idea?
options: The knight on c3 does nothing; via d2 it reaches f3 and attacks e5, and the c-pawn can play c3
White defends against a mating attack on the first rank
White prepares to castle queenside
White offers a draw by repetition
sections.explanation: 24.Nb1 improves the worst white piece and frees the c-pawn. In the game 26.c3 pushed the black knight from b4, 28.Nd2 and 29.Nf3 followed, and 31.Qe6 tied Black down.

sections.question: Karpov-Unzicker, move 24. Karpov played 24.Ba7. Why put the bishop on a7, in front of Black's rook on a8?
options: To block the a-file so White can double rooks behind the bishop and Black can never contest the file
To win the rook on a8 next move
To attack the black king along the diagonal
To defend the pawn on b4
sections.explanation: The a-file is the only open file. With the bishop on a7, Black's rook cannot challenge it, and White's rooks take the file for good. Stockfish 16 at depth 22 rates 24.Ba7 as the best move too (about +0.8). Unzicker resigned after 44.Nh5 (Stockfish 16: about +5.5 for White).
